questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: If I had more time, I would cook dinner every night.
If I have more time, I would cook dinner every night.
If I had more time, I will cook dinner every night.
If I would have more time, I would cook dinner every night.
questions.explanation: Second conditional: If + past simple, would + base verb: 'If I had more time, I would cook dinner every night.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: If she followed the recipe, she wouldn't have burnt the cake.
If she had followed the recipe, she wouldn't burn the cake.
If she would have followed the recipe, she wouldn't have burnt the cake.
If she had followed the recipe, she wouldn't have burnt the cake.
questions.explanation: Third conditional: If + past perfect, would have + past participle: 'If she had followed..., she wouldn't have burnt...'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: This dish is served with rice in most restaurants.
This dish serves with rice in most restaurants.
This dish is serving with rice in most restaurants.
This dish serve with rice in most restaurants.
questions.explanation: Present simple passive: is/are + past participle: 'is served with rice.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The cake ruined because of the high oven temperature.
The cake was ruin because of the high oven temperature.
The cake is ruined because of the high oven temperature.
The cake was ruined because of the high oven temperature.
questions.explanation: Past simple passive: was/were + past participle: 'was ruined because of the high temperature.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The chef which prepared this menu trained in Paris.
The chef who prepared this menu trained in Paris.
The chef whom prepared this menu trained in Paris.
The chef, who prepared this menu, trained in Paris but.
questions.explanation: 'Who' introduces a defining relative clause about a person: 'The chef who prepared this menu...'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: This restaurant which opened last month is already popular but.
This restaurant, which opened last month, is already popular.
This restaurant, that opened last month, is already popular.
This restaurant which opened last month, is already popular.
questions.explanation: Non-defining relative clauses use commas and 'which' for things: 'This restaurant, which opened last month, is already popular.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: That can't being fresh, it smells strange.
That cann't be fresh, it smells strange.
That can't be fresh, it smells strange.
That can't to be fresh, it smells strange.
questions.explanation: 'Can't' + base verb expresses a confident negative deduction: 'that can't be fresh.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The soup could be too salty for some guests.
The soup could to be too salty for some guests.
The soup coulds be too salty for some guests.
The soup could being too salty for some guests.
questions.explanation: 'Could' + base verb expresses a possible deduction: 'the soup could be too salty.'

questions.topic: Present perfect vs present perfect continuous
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I'm trying five different recipes this month already.
I've been trying five different recipes this month.
I've tried five different recipes this month.
I've try five different recipes this month.
questions.explanation: Present perfect simple is used for a completed number of results: 'I've tried five recipes.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I've been baking bread for two hours.
I've baked bread since two hours.
I'm baking bread for two hours already.
I've been bake bread for two hours.
questions.explanation: Present perfect continuous emphasizes duration of an unfinished action: 'I've been baking... for two hours.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence. (Direct: "I have finished cooking.")
options: She said that she has finished cooking.
She said she have finished cooking.
She said that she finished cooking already.
She said that she had finished cooking.
questions.explanation: In reported speech, present perfect shifts back to past perfect: 'she had finished cooking.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence. (Direct: "What ingredients do you need?")
options: He asked me what ingredients I needed.
He asked me what ingredients do I need.
He asked me what ingredients did I need.
He asked me what ingredients I need.
questions.explanation: Reported questions use normal word order (no auxiliary inversion) and shift the tense back: 'he asked me what ingredients I needed.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I use to cook pasta every Friday as a student.
I used to cook pasta every Friday as a student.
I was used to cook pasta every Friday as a student.
I used to cooking pasta every Friday as a student.
questions.explanation: 'Used to' + base verb describes a past habit that no longer happens: 'I used to cook pasta every Friday.'

questions.topic: Be used to / get used to
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I'm used to cook for a large family now.
I use to cooking for a large family now.
I'm used to cooking for a large family now.
I'm used cooking to for a large family now.
questions.explanation: 'Be used to' is followed by a gerund: 'I'm used to cooking for a large family.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Chop the vegetables up before frying them.
Chop up the vegetables before frying them.
Chop up to the vegetables before frying them.
Chop the vegetables before up frying them.
questions.explanation: 'Chop up' means 'cut into small pieces': 'chop up the vegetables.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Heat up the soup before serving it.
Heat the soup up to before serving it.
Heat up to the soup before serving it.
Heat the soup before serving up it.
questions.explanation: 'Heat up' means 'make something hot again': 'heat up the soup.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Despite of the mistake, the dish tasted delicious.
Although the mistake, the dish tasted delicious.
Despite the mistake was big, the dish tasted delicious.
Despite the mistake, the dish tasted delicious.
questions.explanation: 'Despite' is followed by a noun phrase (no 'of'): 'Despite the mistake, the dish tasted delicious.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: She added too much salt, as a result the soup was inedible.
As a result she added too much salt the soup was inedible.
She added too much salt. As a result, the soup was inedible.
She added too much salt as a result, the soup was inedible.
questions.explanation: 'As a result' starts a new sentence and is followed by a comma: 'She added too much salt. As a result, the soup was inedible.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: We don't have flour enough to make bread.
We don't have enough flour to make bread.
We don't have enough of flour to make bread.
We hasn't enough flour to make bread.
questions.explanation: 'Enough' comes before the noun it modifies: 'enough flour.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: My grandmother is really fond at baking.
My grandmother is really fond to baking.
My grandmother is really fond for baking.
My grandmother is really fond of baking.
questions.explanation: 'Fond of' + noun/gerund means 'liking something a lot': 'fond of baking.'

questions.question: Which is the correct way to start an email to a restaurant you haven't visited, asking about a reservation?
options: Hiya,
Dear Sir or Madam,
Hey there,
Yo,
questions.explanation: 'Dear Sir or Madam,' is a suitable formal opening when the recipient's exact name is unknown.

questions.question: Which is the correct way to end a formal email to a named restaurant manager?
options: Talk soon,
Best regards,
Later,
Yours faithfully,
questions.explanation: 'Best regards,' is a suitable semi-formal closing when writing to a named professional contact.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I was wondering could you recommending a good recipe.
I was wondering if you could to recommend a good recipe.
I was wondering if you could recommend a good recipe.
I wonder if you recommend could me a good recipe.
questions.explanation: 'I was wondering if you could' + base verb is a polite way to make a request: 'if you could recommend a good recipe.'

questions.question: Which sentence correctly combines 'This is the chef.' and 'The chef's restaurant won an award.'?
options: This is the chef who restaurant won an award.
This is the chef's restaurant who won an award.
This is the chef which restaurant won an award.
This is the chef whose restaurant won an award.
questions.explanation: 'Whose' shows possession in a relative clause: 'the chef whose restaurant won an award.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I have tasted such a delicious soup never before.
Never I have tasted such a delicious soup before.
I have never tasted such a delicious soup before.
I have tasted never such a delicious soup before.
questions.explanation: 'Never' is placed between the auxiliary and the past participle: 'I have never tasted such a soup.'

questions.question: Which sentence has correct punctuation?
options: I'd like to know whether the restaurant is open tonight?
I'd like to know, whether the restaurant is open tonight.
I'd like to know whether is the restaurant open tonight?
I'd like to know whether the restaurant is open tonight.
questions.explanation: Reported/indirect statements use normal word order and end with a full stop, not a question mark.

questions.question: This time tomorrow, I ___ dinner for the guests.
options: will cook
cook
am cooking
will be cooking
questions.explanation: Future continuous describes an action in progress at a specific future time: 'will be cooking'.

questions.question: By the end of the evening, we ___ three courses.
options: will serve
are serving
will have served
serve
questions.explanation: Future perfect describes an action completed before a future point: 'will have served'.

questions.question: Choose the sentence that correctly uses discourse markers.
options: Firstly we chop onions secondly heat finally garlic.
Firstly, chop the onions. Secondly, heat the oil. Finally, add the garlic.
Finally chop the onions, firstly heat, secondly add garlic.
Secondly firstly chop onions, finally heat oil.
questions.explanation: Discourse markers 'Firstly,', 'Secondly,' and 'Finally,' organize points clearly with commas.

questions.question: Choose the correct question tag.
options: You wouldn't forget the recipe, wouldn't you?
You wouldn't forget the recipe, will you?
You wouldn't forget the recipe, do you?
You wouldn't forget the recipe, would you?
questions.explanation: Negative statement with 'would' + positive tag: 'you wouldn't forget..., would you?'
